samples.hyp: Evaluating the required testing rates for SARS-CoV-2 screening to control outbreaks in Lusaka Province, Zambia, considering asymptomatic individuals:
Simple statistical analysis.

The novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa is characterized by a very large number of asymptomatic (or mildly symptomatic) individuals, who are thought to play an asymptomatic role in the spread of the disease.
The extent and direct contribution of asymptomatic individuals to transmission remains unclear.
However, the research indicates that their behavior is crucial in controlling the transmission of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a simplified deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) mathematical model to explore the impact of active isolation of asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals by examining a control intervention strategy for the Lusaka Province outbreak in Zambia.
Here we compare two scenarios; (1) it is assumed that asymptomatic individuals account for 70% of all COVID-19 cases and (2) asymptomatic individuals account for only 50% of cases.

Conversely, the model was first tested under the assumption that asymptomatic individuals are equally infectious as symptomatic individuals and, secondly, and possibly, under the assumption that asymptomatic individuals are half as infectious as symptomatic individuals.

In a model assuming 70% asymptomatic cases, a sustained minimum daily testing rate of ≥7911 tests/100,000 population would suffice to control the outbreak if asymptomatic individuals constituted only a fraction of transmission; whereas if asymptomatic transmission was assumed to be equal, a testing rate of ≥10028 tests/100,000 population would be required.
With 50% asymptomatic cases, low screening rates of ≥ 4540 per 100,000 population are insufficient to control outbreaks at both the estimated asymptomatic and symptomatic infection rates.
Discussion and conclusion

Our model predicts that active case finding of COVID-19, including asymptomatic individuals, using community testing could be used as a measure to control the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but would come at a high cost.
Testing in large cities like Lusaka could curb the spread of COVID-19, but is it effective?
In 2020, computer models predicted that the spread of COVID-19 in large cities could be better controlled by widespread testing, followed by isolation of all those testing positive.
However, researchers say this method may be expensive and ineffective.
In the early stages of the pandemic, many people infected with COVID-19 did not show symptoms of the disease and still spread the infection to others.
Other research suggests that 50% to 80% of people with COVID-19 were asymptomatic and may be responsible for 40% to 70% of new infections.
Researchers sought to determine whether identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help control the spread of COVID-19.
They also wanted to know whether population-based screening, meaning the unscheduled testing of many people, successfully identifies asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers developed a computer model that predicts how individuals move through the stages of exposure, infection, and isolation.
They focused on data from Lusaka Province in Zambia, a business hub with an international airport located on a border crossing between two countries.

Because the characteristics of COVID-19 appeared to vary geographically, they considered four scenarios, where 50% or 70% of COVID-19 cases were asymptomatic, and these cases were equally or half as infectious as symptomatic cases.
The researchers' model found that it is possible to control the spread of COVID-19 by conducting widespread testing and isolating all individuals who test positive, even those without symptoms.
They stated that to reduce the high number of cases by 90% in all situations, 10% of the Lusaka population needs to be tested daily.
They further found that to keep the number of new COVID-19 infections unchanged, 22% of the population needs to be tested daily.
Although Zambia implemented numerous measures to curb COVID-19, cases continued to rise.
A fabric mask trial successfully reduced the number of COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small Italian town.
However, no previous studies suggest that it will work well in a large city elsewhere.

Note that researchers did not conduct a cloth mask trial in this study; instead they developed a model suggesting that cloth mask use could be effective in reducing the spread of COVID-19 in large cities.
However, they warned that it would likely be very expensive.
They also stated that it may be more effective when combined with other methods, such as lockdowns, contact tracing, and vaccination.
Researchers in Zambia further emphasized that cases of asymptomatic COVID-19 appeared to be more common in Africa at that time.
Low prevalence of certain genetic markers in African populations due to genetic and environmental variations.
African populations are underrepresented in genetic studies but possess high genetic diversity and face a broad range of environmental exposures globally.

Because systematic genome-wide prediction studies had not been conducted in populations encompassing African diversity, we calculated polygenic risk scores (PRS) in a pan-African simulation and in a validation cohort from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to better understand the generalizability of genetic studies.
The accuracy of PRS improves with collections of findings matched to ancestry compared to those from unrelated ancestral studies.
For South African individuals of diverse ancestry, we find that PRS accuracy is low across all traits but varies across groups.
The ancestry of African populations has a greater impact on the accuracy of PRS than other major group differences considered, such as between UK and Ugandan populations.

We developed a PRS for Africans using only existing European-ancestry studies compared to ancestral ones; increased diversity yielded substantially improved accuracy gains for hemoglobin concentration and white blood cell count, reflecting the informative diversity of ancestral variants known to influence sickle cell trait and inflammatory response, respectively.
The variation in PRS accuracy across all African ancestries from different regions is as large as that across all non-African ancestries, necessitating comparable stratification.
Why are we unable to accurately predict genetic diseases in African populations?
Researchers say that current methods used to predict whether a person will develop sickle cell disease are not effective for people of African descent.
This is because the data underlying these predictions often describes the genetic makeup of people of European descent.
The acronym GWAS stands for Genome-Wide Association Studies, and scientists use them to investigate traits and diseases based on genetics.
In fact, they can use GWAS to calculate a person's genetic risk for a disease or trait.
Most of the genetic contribution in GWAS, however, comes from people of European ancestry.
In this study, the researchers sought to determine whether the statistical methods they used to identify genetic risk using GWAS are applicable to people of African descent.
They also sought to determine whether a more diverse GWAS, in other words, a dataset incorporating more African genetic information, could improve prediction.
The measure is more scientifically known as “Polygenic Risk Scores”, or PRS.
They used computers to calculate predicted genetic risks for Africans using GWAS, and used African medical records to look for specific traits or diseases that might be caused by genetic changes.
Using a European GWAS, they found that genetic risk scores were more accurate for individuals of European ancestry compared to those of African ancestry across multiple traits.
They stated that the risk levels were very low among African populations due to population heterogeneity, which is inconsistent with what is observed in European populations.
They also stated that PRS accuracy increases as African ancestry decreases.
Ethiopians had better predictions of genetic diseases as they are more genetically similar to Europeans.
When using a more diverse GWAS including individuals of African ancestry, prediction accuracy improved.
Blood disease prediction was highly accurate.
Previous research has shown that PRS is lower in people of African ancestry, meaning that GWAS data predicts a lower risk of genetic diseases in people of African ancestry.
But we know that this is not entirely true.

This study suggests that these low polygenic risk scores are due to the underrepresentation of African genomes in GWAS datasets, therefore current PRS values are not effective in predicting polygenic diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be beneficial to utilize diverse datasets, including genetic information from African populations.
Therefore, further GWAS work is needed that includes African ancestry to accurately predict the risk of genetic diseases in people of African descent.
The authors of this study were from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
Visual Inspection and Cytology Screening in the Prevention of Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
An estimated 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) which may cause cervical cancer.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy were tested for effectiveness.
However, information related to the impact of cervical cancer screening programs is lacking.
This study investigated the performance of visual inspection and cytology screening in preventing cervical intraepithelial lesions (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.
Findings showed that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia were at increased risk of being screened positive for VIA.
Older women, especially those with HIV, have a higher likelihood of developing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
The VIA procedure appears effective in screening, although colposcopy follow-up of patients in the Namibian context needs to be reviewed and implemented with good HR-HPV results.
Screening methods incorporating HPV testing across different age groups and risk populations (e.g., HIV, immunocompromised individuals) are recommended.

The use of the test can be further improved through interventions using a model that incorporates previous diagnostic results, women's health goals, current knowledge and best practices within the national context.
Women in Namibia at risk of cervical cancer should be screened and treated early.
Many tests can show a woman's risk of cervical cancer, but routine screening in Namibia does not always utilize these tests.
Researchers suggest that regular screening to detect warning signs early could prevent women from developing this deadly disease.
Breast cancer (cancer of the lower part of the breast) causes many deaths in women worldwide.
One of the most common causes of cervical cancer is Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that damages the cervical tissues, creating lesions that can eventually become cancerous.
Although the goal of preventing HPV exists, many women in African countries, including Namibia, cannot access it.
This means that screening for the virus or the lesions it causes is crucial for these women, as it is the best way to help prevent cancer.
Researchers in this study therefore suggest that hospitals require appropriate guidelines and knowledge regarding the best tests to be used.
Furthermore, healthcare workers need more information on how factors such as age or health status affect a woman's risk of developing HPV and cancer.
They investigated how other common types of testing (so-called screening methods) would perform in detecting HPV and lesions.
They also had an interest in comparing testing methods, for example, collecting cells from the placenta to assess damage compared to simply observing lesions.
They also wanted to know whether differences between women, such as their age, or whether they had other diseases such as HIV, changed the chances of getting HPV and cancer.
This knowledge can help hospitals and clinics to implement testing methods effectively.
Researchers reviewed patient records of 214 women screened and treated for HPV, lesions, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
They focused primarily on early-stage cervical cancer, where the disease is most easily and successfully treated.
They also collected information on each woman's age and general health.

By reviewing these records, they found that different screening methods commonly provide healthcare workers with different information, and that they may be most helpful before or after HPV develops into cancer.
Cancer, for example, was often detected by collecting and examining cervical cells.
Lesions, however, were frequently detected by visual examination, using a method called “visual inspection with acetic acid” (VIA).
The advantage of this method is that it allows doctors to detect lesions quickly and at low cost.
This is because it uses basic medical equipment already used in the examination of women's health, such as a speculum (an instrument used to examine the inside of the vagina).
They also found that combining different methods often provides doctors with more information about a woman's risk of developing cancer, especially with more frequent testing.
Furthermore, researchers found that older women, especially those with HIV, have a higher risk of developing cancer, therefore regular screening is crucial.
Researchers added that very few women were screened for HPV (prior to lesion examination) despite the availability of screening.
Doing so could be a crucial way to detect this disease early.

In summary, they stated that their results show a need for the Namibian health system to plan for HPV and cervical cancer prevention strategies thoughtfully, using cheap, effective screening methods for early detection of these diseases.
This study was a collaboration between scientists from Namibia and South Africa.
The benefit of treating concurrent HBV/HIV infection compared to HBV monoinfection in a South African cohort.

Driven by global goals to eliminate hepatitis B virus (HBV), we plan to separate individuals with HBV alone compared to those co-infected with HBV and HIV, to analyze the impact of treatment and monitor progress in healthcare.
We report the findings from an observational study of a mixed, real-world cohort of 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
HIV and another infection were present in 39 (34%) of the study participants.
We recorded mixed populations of laboratory health personnel.

Compared to those with HIV coinfection, older adults with HBV monoinfection were less likely to be HBeAg-positive (p=0.01), less likely to have undergone elastography (p<0.0001), and less likely to have received antiviral treatment (p<0.0001); they were more likely to have HBV viraemia (p=0.04), and more likely to have liver disease features including moderate/severe thrombocytopaenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and an elevated APRI score (p=0.02).
Three cases of hepatocellular carcinoma all arose from HBV infection alone.
Our findings reveal that individuals with HBV alone experienced less vulnerability compared to those with HIV and another condition, highlighting disparities in reporting, referral, and treatment.
Researchers provide guidelines to improve hepatitis B treatment.

In a recent study, researchers were able to clarify that co-infection with both hepatitis B (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) can lead to a more effective treatment response than HBV infection alone.
In Southern Africa, concurrent infection with both HBV and HIV is a major problem.
Doctors need to understand how these viruses and the medications used to treat them interact, so that they can better diagnose diseases and care for patients.
Researchers sought to compare treatment outcomes in patients with HBV alone, and patients with both HBV and HIV.
In this study, researchers recruited 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were recruited at Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients were infected with HIV (39), while others were infected with HBV only.
Researchers considered race, age, and sex, and then performed several health and laboratory assessments.

They found that patients with HBV alone had a lower probability of receiving treatment than those without, suggesting a natural disease course of liver disease (as HBV is a virus that can lead to severe liver disease).

Researchers were able to show that individuals with HBV alone had worse outcomes compared to those with both HIV and HBV, as patients infected with both viruses had access to HIV treatment, which provides an indirect benefit in combating HBV.

Results from this study clarify the potential impact of differences between reporting, screening, and treatment options for HBV when compared to the simultaneous management of HIV and HBV, affecting those co-infected with both HIV and HBV.
Researchers highlight the need to improve and provide safe and effective care for patients with HBV alone.
One limitation of this study was the small sample size confined to a single country and its hospital systems.
Some, perhaps more complex hospital systems may show contradictory findings compared to those found in this study.
Further research may be needed to fully elucidate the differences found in this study.
This paper demonstrated collaborative strength, with researchers working on this project in South Africa and the United Kingdom.
Using South African patients in this study addresses the underrepresentation of Africans.
Furthermore, the research could help develop better treatment strategies for those affected by HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessment of the Impact of Insecurity on Women's Business Activities in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State.

This study investigated the impact of insecurity on the business activities of women in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing on issues related to women's financial constraints, the types of businesses common among them, and the extent of the impact of insecurity on their businesses.
A sample of 377 women was surveyed, leading to the finding that women entrepreneurs in Shiroro have a high level of financial independence and are heavily involved in SMEs.

The study also found that although insecurity negatively impacts women's business operations in terms of financial losses or decline, amongst other things, the number of women entrepreneurs did not significantly decrease.

The study recommends that robust programs to improve women's access to and use of financial services should be developed, and community policing organizations should also be developed and strengthened to address insecurity in the study area.
Women entrepreneurs in Niger need more protection.
Researchers found that female entrepreneurs in Niger are business-minded and financially independent, but safety concerns are a problem.

Researchers sought to determine the safety and security levels of women entrepreneurs in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, and how this might impact their businesses and financial independence.
We interviewed 377 women in this area about the challenges they face regarding their businesses, financial dependence, and insecurity.
They reported that 43% of women said they did not rely on men for money, 32% said they had other people they relied on for money.
Researchers also found that 85% of women earned income from various businesses, with few relying on salaries.
About 56% earned income from farming, and 79% earned income from trading.
Approximately one in five women earned income through hairdressing, sewing, knitting or washing.
The majority of women (91%) told researchers that their businesses were affected due to fear of attacks by thieves and criminals.
They lose money, even their husbands, due to this violence, sometimes forcing them to raise their children alone.
These women also said that they lacked the skills and sufficient capital to grow their businesses.
Researchers reported that despite these challenges, Nigerien women continued to perform very well in their businesses.
They said Shiroro has people of different tribes and religions, and this also helps businesses.
This study challenges the findings of other researchers who reported that women have lower business success rates due to being primary caregivers at home.
Instead, these researchers argue that the success of women entrepreneurs in this Nigerien area is significantly impacted by the threat of criminal attacks and theft.
Researchers recommend that all stakeholders should collaborate to address the challenges hindering business success.
For example, women in Niger need increased access to income-generating opportunities, land, and security.
They further suggested that women in business could form groups to help them combat thieves and criminals.
Serum Selenium, Copper and Zinc Concentrations During Pregnancy are Associated with the Risk of Spontaneous Abortion Before 20 Weeks of Gestation: A Case-Control Study from Malawi
Preterm birth is defined as birth before the completion of 37 weeks of gestation.
The study was conducted to investigate the association between maternal serum selenium, copper and zinc levels, and preterm birth.
There were 181 women in this study where the individual was known by name. 90/181 (49.7%) had reached menopause, while 91/181 (50.3%) had not yet reached menopause.
The mean serum selenium concentration was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, copper was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L and zinc was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L with ranges of 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
Results show that there was no selenium deficiency, and zinc and high serum ferritin levels during pregnancy.
Preterm birth is associated with higher levels of copper and zinc in maternal serum.
Zinc, copper and selenium supplementation before conception.
Researchers found lower serum selenium, copper and zinc levels in women who experienced preterm birth, but it is unknown whether this lower level originates from their diet.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth before 37 weeks of gestation.
Preterm birth is associated with adverse health outcomes in infants from infancy to death.
There may be many causes of premature ejaculation, but the role of low dietary intake of essential fatty acids is not well understood.
This micronutrient is essential for child development, but researchers want to know what happens when it is present in excess.

In this study, researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who had preterm births, and then identify the possibilities that preterm birth is caused by high levels of each of the studied minerals.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women immediately postpartum at two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital city of Malawi, between June 2016 and March 2017.
Blood samples were transported to a laboratory in Norway where serum, the liquid component of blood, was extracted and the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc were measured.
Approximately half of the women in the study had been pregnant previously, and researchers found significantly higher levels of selenium, lead, and zinc.

They adjusted their statistics to account for other factors such as age, health status, and history of pregnancy to disentangle the purported effects of these less significant covariates on preterm birth.
They concluded that high levels of lead and cadmium did not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, but that high levels of zinc increased the risk of preterm birth by more than 6 times.
High levels of the toxin caused concern among researchers, due to its known toxic effects.
Having only 181 women participate in the study limited the researchers' ability to accurately identify thresholds associated with high levels of salinity, as the ideal sample size was 600.
The participants' daily diets were not assessed to identify potential sources of these micronutrients, and their Body Mass Index (BMI) was not recorded.
This is the first study of its kind to assess the effects of selenium, iron, and zinc on pregnant women in Malawi.
Africa has one of the highest rates of preterm birth globally—over 18% compared to 5% in Western countries—so researchers want to know if socioeconomic factors play a role.
Home Range, Site Fidelity, and Habitat Use of the Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals exhibit unique spatial and temporal behaviors that enhance their survival.
Understanding such behavior is a crucial step in the successful conservation and management of particularly endangered animals.

In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of the Pancake trap in the home when deployed and explored the fidelity and habitat use of wildlife species inhabiting natural areas in Kitui County, Kenya.

The behaviour of 39 bee colonies inhabiting 12 isolated rock outcrops was studied from July 2020 to June 2022 using radio tracking, camera trapping, and a combination of group-level scan sampling and ad libitum sampling.

Fourteen individuals were fitted with radio-transmitters and translocated from their natal territories to unfamiliar territories far from their home ranges, and their movements and behaviour were monitored.

Except for only two females that successfully habituated to the new migratory sites, all the others attempted to return home, with 46.15% following their return route to their home sites accurately and 15.38% also reaching areas believed to be within their home range.
Home success provides strong evidence of site fidelity within a species.

Analysis of the occupancy of the bat roosts showed that there was no statistically significant difference between the initial number of bats present in the roosts and the average number present during the 162 days of sampling (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P > 0.05), further supporting the strong site fidelity of the species.
On the other hand, camera trapping events and ad libitum sampling further confirmed that pancake tortoises are a resource that males aggressively defend against other males.
Lost pancake crumbs have an unusual ‘homing’ ability.

Researchers made a surprising discovery while studying the homing behaviour of the East African pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals are able to find their way back home after being displaced long distances.
Understanding how they do this and why it is important for the conservation of these rare and elusive animals.
The way these pigeons find their way home is called “homing”, and many other animals can do this as well.
The ability to return to specific locations allows animals to return to food sources, mates, and shelter, improving their chances of survival and reproduction.

Although the behavior of estuarine fish has been studied in estuaries and clean waters, researchers in this study say that very little is known about their residence in refugia (habitat patches analogous to refuges).
In this study, researchers sought to gain a deeper understanding of the behaviour of pancake tortoises in their natural habitat in the rocky areas of Kenya.
Researchers studied the animals as they moved and fed, and where they rested in burrows, or crevices in the rock.
Researchers observed groups of baboon troops for approximately two years, and set up cameras to record video footage of the animals when they were not directly observing them.
They also attached radio transmitters to 14 of the birds.
These small devices allow researchers to track animal movements, and monitor where they spend their time during the day and night.
Researchers then moved some of these tracked individuals to a new location for easier study.
However, surprisingly to the researchers, two of the birds began returning to their original locations, within 1 to 2.5 kilometers of where they had been removed.
It was at this time that the researchers decided to try removing many animals from their homes, to see if they would exhibit similar 'homing' behaviour.
Before they were transported, they usually walked more than 1.5 km to get there.
Another 15% were able to return to their original location, but did not recover the offspring they had initially taken.
Researchers also found that different ant species generally have a similar number of resting ants, suggesting that ants consistently use the same resting sites.
Images from cameras also showed that male territories were defended, meaning that they fought with other males attempting to enter their territory or mating sites.

Researchers say this is the first time homing behaviour has been observed in pancake studies, and their results show that these animals prefer to stay and rest in the same locations whenever possible.
Their research did not describe the characteristics of the migrations.  To find the way home, therefore future research should focus on understanding this crucial point.
Because animals sometimes need to be moved to new locations for conservation, this information will help conservationists keep the herds safe in their new environment.
This study was a collaboration between Kenyan and Chinese scientists, and it added to our knowledge of the behaviour of bats and other animals.
Plasma Pharmacokinetics of high-dose oral versus intravenous Rifampicin in patients with tuberculous meningitis:
Uncontrolled trial
High-dose rifampicin in the cerebrospinal fluid may improve outcomes for tuberculous meningitis but is not recommended for routine use in high-burden settings.
It was hypothesized that plasma rifampicin levels would be similar between a 35mg/kg oral dose and a 20mg/kg intravenous dose, which was proposed to be tested for efficacy in tuberculous meningitis.
We conducted an open-label, parallel-group pharmacokinetic study nested within a randomized controlled trial of an anti-tuberculosis treatment for cerebral tuberculosis.
Participants with HIV and tuberculous meningitis from South African hospitals were assigned to one of three rifampicin dose groups:
Standard (oral 10mg/kg), high dose (oral 35mg/kg), and intravenous (20mg/kg).
A large pharmacokinetic sample was taken on day 3.
The data were analyzed using noncompartmental analysis; exposure was compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants provided pharmacokinetic samples (standard oral dose, n=17; high oral dose, n=15; intravenous, n=14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The mean rifampicin area under the curve from time zero to 24 hours (AUC0–24) values were 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) for the standard dose, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) for the high oral dose, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) for intravenous administration.

The rifampicin AUC0–24 GMR was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21); the maximum serum drug concentration (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for high-dose oral administration relative to intravenous administration.
Plasma rifampicin AUC0–24 was higher after a 35-mg/kg oral dose than after a 20-mg/kg intravenous dose during the first few days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The findings support the oral dose of rifampicin in the future testing of tuberculous meningitis.
High-dose pills can be tested in patients with HIV and cerebral TB.
Researchers have confirmed the feasibility of initiating a study to determine whether high doses of rifampicin can rescue patients with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis.
Three out of every five HIV patients who also contract cryptococcal meningitis die from this disease, which attacks the nervous system.
Survivors often experience permanent damage to their central and peripheral nervous systems.
This could affect their emotions and movements.
Some patients experience numbness or paralysis, or have impaired function of parts of their face or body.
Rifampicin, a potent anti-tuberculosis drug, is commonly administered as a pill to attempt to kill the bacteria causing tuberculous meningitis.
Severely ill patients often find it difficult to swallow pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously (in infusions) in liquid form.
Then a needle is inserted into the patient's veins to extract fluid from the body.
No tests have been conducted to determine how the patient's body absorbs the medication when this method is used.
Injection treatment requires multiple tools, hospitalization, and a trained healthcare professional who knows how to properly administer an intravenous injection.
Therefore, it is not a feasible approach in areas lacking all necessary resources.
Doctors now know that rifampicin does not penetrate well into cerebrospinal fluid, bone, and abscesses, where bacteria can hide.
Therefore, high doses (concentrations) are needed to effectively kill all the viruses in the patient's body.
However, researchers were unsure how effective and safe a higher dose would be.

Therefore, researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom sought to determine, using a small number of patients, whether it was safe to administer high doses of rifampicin orally or intravenously, and how their bodies would handle each route of administration.
It is important to know this before other researchers begin large-scale trials, or studies, where they plan to give many patients high doses of rifampicin.
One of three rifampicin treatment regimens was given to 46 South African patients with HIV and tuberculous meningitis.
The initial treatment was the standard current pill regimen given to patients, comprising 10mg of rifampicin per kilogram of patient body weight.
One group received tablets of 35 milligrams per kilogram of patient weight.
The third group received a dose of 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
Blood samples were taken from patients after three days.
Researchers then measured the amount of rifampicin present in their blood plasma (the liquid component of blood).
Higher rifampicin concentrations were found in the bodies of patients who received high-dose pills than in those who received intravenous or standard-dose treatment.
Drug plasma concentrations were similar for high-dose and intravenous administration.
This concentration was higher than when patients received only the standard dose.
According to researchers, this indicates that the outcome for patients with tuberculous meningitis could be improved if they receive higher doses of rifampicin.
It doesn't matter whether they receive it as pills or through injections – what is important is that they receive high doses, because their bodies are able to maintain its high concentration.
The results support those found in trials conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
Two small trials in Indonesia, for example, suggested that the lives of many patients could be saved if they were given high doses of rifampicin orally or intravenously.
Unfortunately, however, the researchers caution that fewer participants were part of this study than initially anticipated, which may compromise their results.
The research was conducted in South Africa.
It supports a trial program to test the suitability of providing high doses of rifampicin to HIV-positive patients with tuberculous meningitis.
It is hoped that such treatment will save more lives in Africa and other parts of the world where tuberculosis of the brain is a major problem.
Can the application of compost and biochar improve the quality of degraded savanna soil along the coast?
Soil degradation is a major challenge to crop production in sub-Saharan Africa.
The positive impact of biochar and compost application on soil fertility has been reported by many authors.

This study investigated the 30-day laboratory incubation of 120 g samples of Haplic Acrisol amended with maize biochar (cbio), rice husk biochar (rbio), coconut husk biochar (coco300 and coco700) or poultry compost; and a compost of rice husk biochar (rcocomp) or maize biochar (cococomp) at a 1% w/w application rate; respectively, to the soil.

In another part of this study, a mixture of chicken manure and rice husk or maize biochar (1% compost + 1% biochar: 1% soil w/w), respectively, was incorporated to investigate its effect on soil respiration, soil pH; microbial soil carbon; cation exchange capacity; total organic carbon; total nitrogen and available nitrogen content.
Biochar and compost applied separately or together, and biochar-compost increased soil pH by 0.28–2.29 pH units compared to the control.
Emissions from rice husk or rice husk biochar, or from maize biochar alone or combined with rice husk biochar, were higher than the untreated control, similar to those amended with biochar alone.
TOC in the single application and biochar amended soils increased by 37% and 117%, respectively, compared to the control.
The application of rice husk biochar mixed with compost increased MBC by 132%, while compost alone increased MBC by 247%, respectively, compared to the untreated soil.

In conclusion, the study showed that the combined or separate application of compost and biochar, or compost biochar, improved soil parameters such as soil pH and MBC, and promoted better soil C sequestration by increasing TOC and reducing soil C loss through respiration.
Biochar and compost improve soil quality for planting.
This study investigated how biochar, a highly porous, carbon-rich charcoal produced from waste biomass, can be used to improve soil quality in sub-Saharan Africa.
Research found that biochar improves soil quality in a manner comparable to other expensive and less readily available methods.
One of the major challenges facing crop production in sub-Saharan Africa is soil fertility decline.
Better soil leads to better harvests, which reduces hunger in rural areas and restores environmental resources to the area.
Research has shown that biochar can be used to improve soil fertility.
Biochar is produced when biomass is burned in an oxygen-deficient environment.
Biochar has been shown to increase soil porosity, enhance water and air availability, and promote soil structure.
This study investigated the impact of biochar and compost on soil quality using indicators such as soil respiration, soil pH, microbial biomass, carbon content, and nitrogen content.

Researchers produced biochar from maize, coconut shells, and rice husks using pyrolysis, which involves the heating of organic matter in an oxygen-deficient environment, at 450 °C in a locally fabricated furnace.

Point-of-care (POC) testing in communities, homes, and primary healthcare facilities is believed to have great potential in reducing delays in diagnosis and treatment initiation for diseases such as HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, and syphilis.

Rapid diagnosis and additional management decisions completed in the same clinical encounter or at least on the same day, while the patient is still waiting, promise to overcome delays associated with conventional laboratory-based testing.
However, the availability of cheap, simple, and rapid tests that can be performed outside of laboratories does not automatically guarantee effective point-of-care (POC) testing.

To understand the new roles and challenges that diagnostic tools like this present, we need research into how diagnostics are used at the point of care (POC) and integrated into workflows and patient pathways.
This chapter reviews selected findings from a large-scale research project on the challenges of point-of-care (POC) testing in India and South Africa and discusses them comparatively.

This project used informal and group discussions to explore diagnostic pathways for all major diseases and actors in homes, clinics, communities, hospitals, and laboratories in South Africa and India.
Comparing the selected results, it is clear that both countries have very different diagnostic systems providing very different POC testing scenarios.
The chapter concludes by considering how to account for such details when designing POC testing programs.

Point-of-care (POC) testing refers to health care testing performed at the same location where the patient receives care, rather than sending patient samples to a laboratory for analysis.
South Africa and India experienced delays in rapid and effective testing due to their poor POC and laboratory infrastructure.

They held discussions and meetings with groups and healthcare workers, patients and medical equipment companies from March 2012 to July 2013 in both countries.
They were asked about the procedures and challenges of POC.

Participants stated that there should be more laboratories in hospitals, and that testing should be done at the same point of entry for patients.

In South Africa, it was found that in the public health system, a single company handles all testing, therefore samples go to this company.
Further basic testing is done on-site, and patients receive results quickly.
HIV and TB testing takes a long time, therefore follow-up or treatment is also delayed.
Other delays were due to transportation issues, incorrect patient sample labeling, mislabeling of samples, and computer system failures.

Regarding the definitions of critical illness and critical care, conceptual analysis was used.

Because "critical illness" and "critical care" lack universally agreed-upon definitions, this study aims to explore how these concepts are used, to describe their defining characteristics, and to propose potential definitions.
We used the slow Walker and Avant method in analyzing the concept.
The use and definitions of concepts were identified through a scoping review of the literature and an online survey of 114 global healthcare professionals.
By analyzing the content of the extracted data, we coded, categorized, and thematically analyzed it to identify indicators that define concepts and propose potential interpretations.
To aid understanding, we present models, related and contrasting cases concerning the concepts, we outline the antecedents and consequences of the concepts, and we cited strong references.
Defining characteristics of critical illness were imminent risk of death; dysfunction of vital organs; need for intervention to prevent death; and potential for reversal.

Critical care indicators included the identification, monitoring, and treatment of critical illnesses; support of vital organs; initial and ongoing care; any critical illness care; and specialized human and physical resources.
Our proposed definition of critical illness is, "a life-threatening condition affecting a vital organ, with a high risk of imminent death if care is not provided and potential for reversal".
Our proposed definition of critical care is, “the identification, monitoring and treatment of patients with critical illness through initial and ongoing support of vital organ functions.”
The definitions of critical illness and critical care lack consensus and have variable applications.

Through a conceptual analysis of usage and definitions in literature and among experts, we identified defining characteristics of the concepts and proposed definitions that could aid clinical practice, research, and policy-making.

Specialized equipment should also not be referenced in the care.

In this chapter, we explore the extent to which research in South Africa is focused on biodiversity loss compared to other aspects of global change.

Using the Web of Science, we systematically reviewed literature relevant to the South African environment published between 2000 and 2018 and pertaining to biological invasions, climate change, overharvesting, habitat alteration, land degradation, and/or atmospheric CO2.
We analyzed 1149 relevant papers scored according to their driver coverage and driver interactions affecting various biota or ecosystem services.
A strong spatio-temporal effect was observed in the research study.
Firstly, efforts varied across regions, where habitat change, land degradation and overharvesting received more research focus on terrestrial, freshwater and marine/coastal habitats respectively.
Secondly, certain globally well-studied topics were not documented in local literature (e.g., fewer than five papers on ocean acidification).
We identified 21 different interactions among drivers, with interactions between invasive species and habitat alteration (e.g., altered fire regimes in invaded areas) being most prominent.
However, less than 4% of the papers discussed interactions between three or more drivers.

This suggests that although the importance of understanding driver interactions is recognised, there has been limited research into the combined effects of driver interactions in South African living environments.

The previously cited statement that invasive species are the second greatest threat to biodiversity conservation, after habitat change, is consistent with the results of research on this driver in South Africa.

Case studies illustrating the reasons and circumstances of female genital cutting/mutilation in Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya.
Female genital mutilation/cutting is a harmful traditional practice that violates women's human rights and has negative health consequences.
This paper presents the reasons and circumstances surrounding female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) in specific areas of three countries – Indonesia, Ethiopia and Kenya.

Data was collected through a household survey involving young people (aged 15-24) and through focus group discussions, in-depth interviews and key informant interviews with youth and community stakeholders during 2016 and 2017.
Descriptive statistics and content analysis of the corpus were performed.
The study results confirm some of the reasons for FGM/C documented in previous research, noting that these reasons are largely interconnected, with gender norms being a primary driver.
In all three scenarios, these factors drive the modification of women's bodies to produce a culturally ‘enhanced’ body that is acceptable within the ancestral context.
This results in a ‘clean body’ in Indonesia, a ‘soft body’ in Ethiopia and an ‘old body’ in Kenya.
Healthcare workers and parents play a crucial role in decision-making regarding FGM/C in all circumstances.
In Kenya, particularly, young women discussed their role in decision-making regarding FGM/C as they matured during the cutting period.

The research reveals how changes in the legal and social contexts in each location have led to variations in FGM/C practices, resulting in the decline of FGM/C in Indonesia, a reduction in the age at which girls are cut in Kenya, and an increasing clandestine practice of FGM/C in Ethiopia.
These three cases demonstrate significant variation in the practice of FGM/C and the social meanings associated with it among young women and their communities.
There is a need to further investigate the role of parents in decision-making.

Due to the interaction between different FGM/C practitioners within each context, the research concludes that context-specific strategies need to be adopted for intervention to achieve lasting change.

In some parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), sometimes called ‘female circumcision’, is still commonly practiced.

In this study, researchers sought to gain a deeper understanding of why FGM occurs in different countries, and what people's beliefs are regarding this practice.
Therefore, they collected information on FGM in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.

In each country, researchers spoke to people involved in this practice, including parents, youth, traditional leaders, healthcare workers, and ‘circumcisers’ (older women who traditionally performed FGM on young girls).
In some instances, they interviewed these individuals individually, but also spoke with groups of people, including older and younger adults who had undergone FGM.
Researchers found that the reasons for FGM, the way it is performed, and beliefs about the practice, vary from country to country.
They also found that many people still practiced it even in areas where it was illegal.
For example, in Indonesia, traditional birth attendants used a knife or needle to cut a part of the clitoris (the female sexual organ) when a girl child was 40 days old.
People believed this helped to ‘remove impurities’ and that it was important for religious reasons.
In Ethiopia, FGM has been practiced even earlier, sometimes when children are only 7 days old.
Researchers found that people believed this would ensure that the girl would become a ‘good wife’ one day, and that she would be obedient and not violent towards her husband.
Many people believe that FGM makes childbirth easier, but in reality it can make childbirth much more difficult.
During that time in Kenya, FGM signified a girl's transition to womanhood, and it was often performed early in life, while she was still young.

In some cases, however, they found that girls could undergo FGM as young as 8 years old, and that many girls end up pregnant at a young age, because they were considered sexually mature enough after FGM.
Researchers say their findings indicate that there are multiple reasons for its occurrence.
As laws and social norms change, so do the ways and places in which things are done.
For example, parents might attempt to do this secretly, even though it is illegal, because they believe it is necessary for their daughter to have good health or find a good husband.
It is important to note that because FGM is illegal in some places, research on the topic may be difficult, and people may not always provide truthful answers about the subject.

In the future, beyond legalization, researchers say governments and health authorities should aim to stop FGM by addressing the misconceptions people have about the practice and educating them about the risks.

This study was a collaboration between scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and is part of a larger program called ‘Yes I do’, aimed at reducing adolescent pregnancy, child marriage, and FGM.

Reproductive Hormone Imbalance, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Significant Alterations in Large African Pouched Rats (Cricetomys gaambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Intoxication
Environmental exposure to vanadium has been increasing recently.
This tool is a known remedy.
The current study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in African giant pouched rats.
SMV was administered intraperitoneally daily for 14 consecutive days at a dose of 3 mg/kg body weight.
Sterile water was given to the control group.
We analyzed serum reproductive hormones, sperm preservation and quality, and ultrastructural changes in the testes after SMV treatment.
Our results showed that the administered SMV group significantly increased progesterone but decreased testosterone, FSH and LH concentrations.

Furthermore, the SMV-treated group showed a statistically significant decrease in sperm motility and a significant increase in the percentage of abnormal spermatozoa morphophenotypes and P53 immunopositive cell counts.
Ultrastructural studies revealed viral vacuolation in Sertoli cells, both cytoplasmic and nuclear; mitochondrial swelling and vacuole extrusion were also observed.
There was extensive seminiferous tubule degeneration, atrophy, and myeloid cell depletion, and apoptosis of Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells.

In conclusion, intraperitoneal SMV exposure has significant adverse effects on several serum reproductive hormones, reducing sperm count and quality, inducing apoptosis, and causing degenerative changes in Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells, which may lead to infertility.
Researchers say that a metal found in polluted air causes mice to be infertile.
Researchers found that vanadium, a type of metal, damages mouse cells and their ability to reproduce.

Because this metal is also toxic to humans, they proposed further research to determine whether the metal, which is increasingly found in the environment due to pollution, may have similar adverse effects on human health.
Even though vanadium is a metal, it can enter the air in small amounts when fuels such as oil and coal are burned.
As the world uses more of these petroleum sources, the amount of vanadium exposure is increasing.
We know that people exposed to it can experience health problems such as anemia, dry cough and eyes, and chest pains.
Recently, scientists have been interested in the effects vanadium may have on reproduction.
They have begun studying these results in mice, which are commonly used in laboratories due to their similarity to humans.
In this study, scientists were interested in the effects of vanadium on a common species of rat found in West Africa, known as the African Giant Rat.
They sought to understand how vanadium alters the reproductive systems of male mice, specifically their testes, hormones, and testicular cells.
Researchers treated 6 male mice with vanadium daily for 14 days.
Simultaneously, they injected another 6 mice with water as a “control” experiment.
Because the water did not affect the mice, the researchers could be certain that any changes they observed in the first six mice were a result of the vanadium injections.
After 14 days, they checked whether the levels of hormones like testosterone had changed, then examined the testes and measured their size.
Using a method called Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), they were able to observe any changes occurring in the lungs in detail, down to the individual cell level.
Researchers found that mice treated with vanadium had significantly lower levels of testosterone and other hormones crucial for reproduction.
The vanadium-treated mice also had significantly smaller testes, and their sperm had reduced viability.
Researchers observed, for example, that one male mouse lacked a head or had a curved tail, and that it did not move as much as a male from the water-deprived mice.
Because sperm are the male gametes in living organisms and are used to fertilize female eggs, these changes could make it significantly more difficult for mice to successfully reproduce.
Finally, researchers found that some cells from mouse livers were severely damaged or destroyed by vanadium.
Researchers said the mutations they found could ultimately lead to infertility.
They noted that since animals exposed to vanadium and other environmental pollutants may be unable to reproduce, they may become extinct due to these effects.
Because humans are mammals like rodents, scientists must also study any potential adverse effects of vanadium in contaminated areas on human health.

Researchers cautioned that some of the anatomical and hormonal changes they observed in the animals differed from those reported in previous scientific studies, therefore further work is needed to understand the damage caused by vanadium.
This study was a collaboration between scientists from Nigeria and Egypt, and it adds to what scientists know about how animals, and perhaps humans, are affected by pollution.
Traditional Use of Indigenous Plants in a North-Western Ethiopian Community
The floral composition of homegardens in Northwest Ethiopia, and the Gozamin district in particular, has received little research attention.
The aim of this study is to better understand the structure and cultural significance of homegardens.
A stratified unclustered sampling procedure was used based on agroecological stratification in the selected wards.

Homegarden data was collected by dividing the homegarden into four quadrats; the first quadrat extending from the farmer's house to 10m, the second from 10m to 20m, the third from 20m to 30m, and the fourth from 30m to 40m, systematically, as a function of garden size.
A structured interview was conducted to document the knowledge of an expert on plant species.
238 culturally important plant species from 81 families were identified.
Of these, 39% were remedies, 29% were plants, and 6% were passengers.
Perennial plants constituted the majority of the cultivated species (83%), while annual plants made up the remainder (17%).
The Poaceae family had the highest number of species, with 22, followed by Fabaceae with 21, and Asteraceae with 15.

Of the recorded plants, 140 (58.6%) were species used for environmental purposes, 84 (35%) were food plants, 83 (34.7%) were medicinal plant species, 39 (16.3%) were fodder species, 57 (23.8%) were fiber plants, 60 (25%) were timber species, 50 (21%) were plants used by the community, and 1 (0.4%) were poisonous.
The direct matrix ranking revealed that *Cordia Africana* was identified as a multi-purpose plant of significant cultural importance and high risk, followed by *Ficus sur*.
A very high number of Cordia africana trees were used for construction and a number were also used for medicinal purposes.
The Sorensen similarity index of 64% of the surveyed sites was below 0.5.
The results showed that homegardens have multiple functions, and long-term production systems.
Food security and biodiversity conservation are continuously supported by the traditional ecological knowledge of indigenous peoples related to their animals.

The low similarity/high diversity of animal species in the inter-village area indicated that there was high species diversity, which was due to the different range of agroecological conditions between villages.
Ethiopian gardens support food security and nutrition.
Researchers say that many people in Ethiopia cultivate food crops, ornamental plants, medicinal plants, and plants providing fodder, shade, or fencing in their gardens.
These crops were analyzed to determine their importance in ensuring food security and contributing to environmental conservation.
Communities worldwide maintain gardens for food production, income generation, and other cultural purposes.
Gardens also protect important plants that are often absent or have disappeared in other areas.
In Ethiopia, there is limited research on what communities plant in their gardens.
In this study, researchers sought to investigate the plants that people in the Gozamin district of Northwest Ethiopia cultivate in their gardens and how they use them.
They identified and counted 357 plants in the garden area.
They also discussed with the community what they use the plants for.
Researchers found that all the gardens in Gozamin were less than one hectare in size.
They collected and identified 238 different plants.
Most plants (83%) were cultivated year-round, and only a few (17%) had specific growing seasons.
Their results showed that the community used plants for food, medicine, building materials, fodder (animal feed), and other cultural uses.
Many plants fulfilled more than one purpose.
For example, a large-leaved northern tree can be used for medicine, ornamentation, fodder, shade, firewood, and other cultural uses.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for environmental purposes such as firewood, fencing, shade and ornamentation.
Researchers said this helps protect the environment.
Irrigation also helped protect the farm yield.
More than one-third (35%) of the plants were harvested for consumption, such as fruits, vegetables, grains and spices.
However, the gardens in this area mainly provide fruits.
Researchers found that 35% of the plants were used as traditional medicine for animal and human wellbeing, while 21% were used for rituals and religious purposes, smoking, spices and baking.
Some plants (17%) were used as fodder to feed cattle, sheep and donkeys.
Others (24%) worked in construction, making garden tools, thatching and making ropes.
Since the majority of rural people are reported to use firewood, 25% of the plants are used for that purpose.
Researchers found that only one plant (0.4%) was intentionally reported for herbicide application.
They also stated that the way plants are distributed in the area is influenced by the environment, people's preferences, and the family's financial situation and business needs.
For example, the Wenka site, which had irrigation and was near a large town, had numerous ponds and recorded 130 different plant species.
The Wenka people also farmed and brought fruit and vegetables to the town market.
Finally, the researchers state that most farmers prefer to cultivate high-demand crops.
Researchers stated that their results confirm that farmers indeed cultivated a greater number of diverse crop types in their gardens, and with different uses.
Although these researchers found that many farmers plant medicinal plants, other researchers say that trees are more common in the area.
The researchers of this study were based at Ethiopian universities.
